title: Chapter 107 – Foundation Middle
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

One year later.

Bai keeps the checklist on a single sheet of paper, pinned to the wall of the Nine Furnace Room, and it has twenty-three lines.

Jian reads it for the fortieth time on the morning of the breakthrough, standing in the doorway with a bowl of plain rice porridge going cold in his hands. The room is round and windowless, built of fire-brick, with nine small clay furnaces set in a ring around a central stone floor. The air smells of ash and camphor. A single oil lamp burns on a tripod. He can feel, in the soles of his feet, the faint warmth of embers banked three days ago and never allowed to die.

One. Qi: step five, steady, three months without drift. Done. He has not felt the river in his channels waver since the autumn.

Two. Body: step five, steady, six months. Done. Kuang has hit him every dawn for three years. On the last day of the last month, she lowered her pole, looked at him with her flat eyes, and said, "Enough." It is the nearest she has come to praise.

Three. Soul: step five, six months stable. Done. The vessel mended on the bench, and the mending set, and in the spring he woke one morning and found it deeper than it had been, and knew.

Four. Spread no more than two steps. Qi will rise to six. Body and soul at five. A spread of one. Within tolerance.

He reads on. Anchor furnace, lit and warmed. Guardian at the door. Medicine at hand. Escape route marked. There is a line for the weather, which Bai has crossed out. A line for the moon. A line that reads, in the old Elder's cramped hand, DO NOT TOUCH THE SECOND FURNACE, YOU IDIOT, and another, below it, smaller: (you know why).

The last is written in a different ink, fresher, and boxed in red.

Twenty-three. The pill.

* * *

It is a very small thing to be so heavy.

He takes it from the inner pocket of his tunic, where it has lain wrapped in oilcloth for three and a half years, and sets it on the stone. It is a gray bead the size of a bean, dull and plain, with a faint dusting of ash on its surface. It does not shine. It does not hum. It looks like something a child might find on a road and throw away.

The Nine Turn pill.

He has carried it since the Mountain Gate. It was the one thing he kept when everything else was spent, a coin held back against the day when nothing else would do. The first time he had taken a pill like it, in the old days, it had cost him a crack down the center of his mind. This one has waited, wrapped in cloth, for the day when the vessel was whole.

"You look at it as if it might bite," says Bai.

The old Elder has come in behind him, silently, in felt slippers, with a plum in each fist and a bundle of herbs under his arm. He looks older than he did. The round face has settled into deep lines. But his small shrewd eyes are exactly as they were, bright as a bird's.

"It might."

"It will not." Bai sets the herbs on the floor. "It will do what it was made to do. Nine waves. Each one a little worse than the last. If you take the first, you will want to stop. If you take the third, you will want to die. By the sixth you will be certain you have made a terrible mistake." He bites the plum. "By the ninth you will either be a Foundation Middle or a cinder. I have never lost a patient. I have never had one who took it with a whole soul, either."

"I am told that helps."

"It helps a great deal. It means that you will feel every wave." Bai grins. "Eat your congee."

* * *

The guard is posted at the door at noon.

It is Kuang, who has not been asked. She arrives with her pole across her shoulder and takes up a position in the corridor outside, with her back to the wall and her arms folded, and when Bai says, mildly, that she might sit, she says, "No." That is all. A silent column of muscle and bone.

Behind her, down the passage, a little knot of people has gathered, and Jian hears them before he sees them. A stir of voices. A cough. The scuff of boots.

He goes to the end of the corridor and looks.

His brother is there, big and quiet in the silver-edged gray of a Silver Leaf, with a new jade pin that marks him a Foundation Middle, and a stubble of beard. Lin Feng is twenty-nine. He has been in the Inner Court for three years, and has become, without any fuss, a man whom other men step aside for. Beside him stands Lin Yue, who is thirteen, taller than she was, with her long black braid down her back and a satchel of herbals over her shoulder, and she is trying very hard not to look as frightened as she is.

And behind them, at a respectful distance, stands Ye.

"We did not come to watch," says Feng at once. "We came to wait."

"Wait where?"

"Here." His brother glances at the floor. "Mother wanted to come. She cannot leave the Garden. She sent a basket." He nods at a cloth-wrapped bundle on the bench. "It is rice and pickles and a note. She says not to read the note until after."

"Feng."

"I know. I know." The big shoulders lift. "I have said every word to myself in the mirror. I will not say them again. I am only going to sit on that bench and stare at the wall until you come out."

Yue steps forward, clutching her satchel.

"Can I give you something?" she says.

She holds out her hand. In it lies a small, flat, folded square of paper. He takes it. When he unfolds it, a sprig of dried silverthread falls into his palm, pressed flat, and a drawing in her careful hand: a leaf, a stem, a root, and under them in tiny letters, for the lungs; for after.

"It quiets the breath," Yue says, in a rush. "If you cannot stop coughing. I tried it on the goat. It works."

"Thank you, Yue."

"It's not much."

"It is exactly what I need." He closes his hand. "I will use it."

He goes back into the Furnace Room, and the door closes behind him on their three faces, and he thinks that of all the things he has carried into this room, the pressed leaf weighs the most.

* * *

He sits on the stone floor in the center of the ring of furnaces, with his legs crossed and the pill in his palm.

Bai has gone. The old Elder stands outside the door with Kuang, and in the closed room there is only the lamp, the banked embers, the quiet. Pebble sits on his knee, silent for once, with its snout pointing at the gray bead as though at a snake.

He opens the Door in Autumn.

It costs two points of CE. He has twenty-eight. He spends them without hesitation, because a man ought to know what he is carrying before he lights it. The world sharpens. The room dims. In the center of his sight he sees himself, lit from within: the Foundation base, a six-sided stone of pale light, steady as a lamp; the nine bright rivers of the channels; the Seal, a five-colored coil under the breastbone, calmer now than it has been in years. The soul vessel, whole, glowing like a bowl of moonlight. The scar on his left arm, dull gray.

And at the base of his skull, the silver thread.

It is as it was. Fine, faint, cold. But tonight there is something different about it. It is not still. It trembles, very slightly, like a leaf in a draft.

It knows, he thinks. It knows what I am about to do.

He does not know how. He does not know who. But he feels the thread tighten, in the way a net tightens when a fish begins to swim, and he understands that the breakthrough will be seen. Not by the Sect, not by the Registry. By whatever is on the other end of that line.

Locator. When queried.

He closes the reading. The room swims back.

"Pebble," he says.

Yes.

"If the thread pulls. If it asks. Tell me what you feel."

I will tell. The pangolin shifts its small weight. I do not like it. It smells like old stone. It smells like the door under the fortieth step.

"I know."

You will do it anyway.

"Yes."

Good. The black eyes are very bright. Then do it fast. I do not like waiting.

He puts the pill on his tongue.

* * *

The first wave is a warmth. It is no worse than the heat of a cup of tea, and it goes down his throat and spreads through his chest like a small friendly sun. For a moment he thinks that Bai has been exaggerating. He breathes. He draws the heat down into the base, into the six-sided stone, and the stone brightens and holds.

The second wave is hotter.

It comes up from the belly like a hand opening, and the heat is no longer friendly. It goes into the channels, into the nine rivers, and each of them flares in turn, bright as molten wire. His skin prickles. Sweat starts at his hairline and runs down into his collar. He keeps his eyes closed. He keeps his breath slow. In his mind he counts, one, two, three, and the base takes the heat and glows.

The third wave is the first that hurts.

It is not like fire. It is like being unmade. Every channel he has opened in the last twenty years, every river and tributary, is struck at once by a blow of white light, and for a moment he feels the whole structure of his Qi shudder like a bell. A sound comes out of him that he does not choose. His hands clench on his knees. He tastes blood.

Three, he thinks. Three of nine.

Wake, says Pebble's small voice, from very far away. Wake. Not sleep. Breathe.

He breathes.

* * *

By the fifth wave, he has stopped counting.

There is only the heat, and the heat is everywhere, and he is a thing in the middle of it, a seed in a furnace. The base is a blaze. The channels are rivers of light. The Seal is a wheel of five colors spinning so fast that it blurs, and the soul vessel hangs above it all, a moon of cold white glass, steady, whole, taking every blow and not cracking.

That is what the bench bought, he thinks, through a haze. That is what forty points of CE were for.

In the sixth wave he screams. He hears it echo in the round room. A great ugly raw sound, with no shape in it, and somewhere beyond the door a voice calls his name and is hushed. His body arches. The sweat on his chest steams. He feels his bones, every one of them, ring like struck iron, and the Iron Bone drill takes the shock and spreads it, through the ribs, the spine, the long bones of the legs, an old patient hammering that has made of him a thing that can bear this.

Kuang, he thinks, absurdly. Thank you.

In the seventh wave he forgets his name.

In the eighth he forgets he is a man.

* * *

The ninth wave is a silence.

It comes after the eighth like the calm in the eye of a storm. The heat is gone. The light is gone. The pain has stopped as a pain stops in a dream, all at once, without leaving a mark, and he finds himself floating in a quiet dark, in a warm gray sea, with nothing above him and nothing below.

The base lies in front of him.

It is no longer a stone. It has opened. It is a flower of six petals, and each petal is a color, white, red, gold, green, black, and a sixth that is no color, only the memory of one. In the center is a bright small point, steady as a star. And around that point, slowly, silently, the Qi of his whole body is turning, ring by ring, as water turns in a bowl.

Liquid, he thinks. The Qi is liquid. It flows.

He feels it run. Through the channels, through the bones, through the marrow and the skin. It is not a river now. It is a sea. It moves with a weight and a depth that the Foundation Early never had, and he understands, with the simple clarity of a man waking from a dream, that this is the thing that men give their lives to reach, and that he has reached it.

Foundation Middle, he thinks.

And then the sky answers.

* * *

It begins as a hum.

He hears it in the stone beneath him, in the clay of the furnaces, in the air itself. A deep low note, rising. It is not a sound that comes from any throat or bell. It comes from the vault above, from the whole bowl of the sky, and it rolls over the mountain like the tolling of a vast soft drum.

Outside, in the Inner Court, a hundred disciples look up.

He does not see it. He cannot. He is in a windowless room, in the dark, with his eyes closed. But Kuang sees it, standing in the corridor with her pole, and says nothing. Feng sees it, from the bench, with his hand on his sword. Yue sees it, at the window, and her mouth falls open. Ye sees it from the stair, and her pale eyes widen, and she lets out a long breath.

Above the Furnace Room, the clouds have parted.

They roll back from a point above the roof like water from a dropped stone, and the winter sky, gray a moment ago, opens to a vault of violet-gold. A beam of light descends. It is not bright. It is the color of tea with the sun behind it, and it falls straight down through the roof and the floor and the stone and the sleeping furnaces, and rests on the boy in the center of the ring.

The disciples of the Inner Court fall silent.

They have seen sky visions before. Everyone has. A Core disciple's breakthrough sometimes draws a ray, and once in a generation a True disciple draws a rain of petals. But a Foundation Middle? At twenty-five? In the space of one afternoon, over an alchemist's furnace, with nothing but a gray bead of pill and a cheap felt cap?

It's an omen, someone whispers.

Of what?

Nobody answers.

* * *

He opens his eyes.

The light is gone. The ring of furnaces stands cold around him, and the lamp has burned out. His tunic is soaked, and his hair is plastered to his skull, and every muscle in his body is trembling. But the quiet is perfect. The sea of Qi turns slowly in his base, deep and calm, and his channels hum with it.

Qi: Foundation Middle, the panel says in the corner of his eye, in small flat letters. Step 6. Body: step 5. Soul: step 5. Spread: 1.

He sits for a long time and does nothing at all.

Then the door opens, and the corridor floods the room with torchlight, and a broad scarred face looks in. Kuang says nothing. She walks across the stone, kneels, and puts two fingers to his wrist, and her mouth moves in what might be the beginning of a smile.

"Bones ring," she says.

"Yes."

"They ring true." She sits back on her heels. "I did not think you would do it."

"You hit me every morning for three years."

"I hit everyone. Most of them break." She stands, and looks down at him with her flat eyes, and says, quite deliberately, "Well done."

* * *

Bai finds him half an hour later, on the bench in the corridor, with a bowl of Mother's rice in his lap and Yue's sprig of silverthread tucked behind his ear. His brother has an arm round his shoulders. Ye stands nearby, saying nothing, with a face like carved ivory.

"Foundation Middle," says Bai, from the doorway. He is out of breath, and flushed, and beaming. "Sixth step. Twenty-five years old. I am going to have to rewrite the Pill Hall's records." He wipes his face with his sleeve. "That is a thing I have been waiting forty years to say."

"Thank you, Elder."

"Do not thank me. We have the matter of the bill." Bai lowers himself onto the end of the bench. "Three nights of the Nine Furnace Room. The lamp oil. The herbs. The anchor ash. Six sticks of Moon-ash incense." His small eyes twinkle. "I have decided that I will take it in kind."

Jian stiffens. "In kind."

"A crucible." The old man spreads his hands. "One. Of the sort you can make on that bench of yours. Pool-grade. Quiet-fire coupled, if the book allows. I have a pill that wants a vessel it cannot have." He smiles. "I do not ask how. I ask only that it be done by the next solstice."

Thirty CE. Possibly more. He does the sum in his head.

"It will be done," he says.

"Good." Bai pats his knee. "Eat your rice. You look like a man who has been born."

* * *

He reads his mother's note in the late afternoon, alone, in the Pill Hall's spare alcove, by the last light of a narrow window.

It is a sheet of paper in her firm round hand, folded in thirds and tucked into the basket under the pickles.

Jian. If you are reading this, you are alive, and the thing is done. I will not ask how it went. I am told that is bad luck. I will only say that I am sitting in the kitchen with a mug I have not drunk, listening for a bell.

The Hall is full today. Your father has stopped working and is walking round the courtyard with his hands behind his back, which he does when he is afraid. Hu is hammering something, although it is the middle of the night. Wenjun says she will not sleep until she hears. I have told her she is an old fool, and she has told me I am a young one.

I did not want to come because I knew I would not be able to stay quiet. You know me. I am not good at waiting.

I want to say a thing that I have not said. You came to us when we had nothing. A boy of ten who did not seem to know how to be a child. I used to lie awake and wonder who you were. I do not wonder now. You are the boy who stood in front of the cradle and the door and the Gate and said, "I will do it." That is enough. That is more than enough.

Whatever you are, you are mine.

Eat the rice. It's still warm, I think.

Mother.

He reads it twice. He folds it small. He puts it inside his tunic, against the skin, beside the pressed sprig of silverthread, and sits for a long time with his hands on his knees, looking at the square of fading light.

The rice is cold. He eats it anyway.

* * *

The summons comes at dusk.

It is carried by a boy in white, a servant of the ridge-houses, who walks up the Pill Hall steps in the last gold light and stops before the Gate Bearer with a bow so deep that his forehead nearly touches the stone. He does not say a word. He holds out both hands, and in them lies a card of heavy white paper, edged with silver, with a single character embossed on the front.

Shen.

Jian takes it. He turns it over. On the back, in a firm, elegant, quite unhurried hand:

A sky like that is not an accident. The Cloud Peak Hall would be honored if the Gate Bearer would join it for tea. At his earliest convenience. — Shen Yuxian, Core disciple.

Beside him on the bench, Feng's hand moves to the hilt of his sword.

"Nine years in seclusion," says Ye, very quietly. She has come up behind them, silent as a cat, and her pale eyes are fixed on the card. "He came out this morning. The Hall's servants say he walked down from the ridge at noon, in the middle of the vision. He stood in the Inner Court's yard and watched the sky until it closed."

"And now he wants tea."

"He wants a look at you."

The boy in white bows again. He waits.

* * *

Qin Hao is waiting at the foot of the Pill Hall steps after the boy in white has gone, with a paper lantern in his hand.

He has aged, in the three years since the council. The beard is white now, the shoulders a little bowed. But he stands very straight, and when Jian comes down the steps with the white-edged card in his fist, the old scholar puts out a hand and takes it without asking, and reads it by the lantern's light.

"Shen Yuxian," he says.

"You know him."

"I know the Cloud Peak Hall. I have known them for sixty years." Qin Hao folds the card once and returns it. "They are polite. They are old. They have never, in all that time, done an unkind thing in public. It is a record of which they are very proud."

"And in private?"

"I do not know." The scholar's voice is dry. "That is what troubles me. Nine years in the ridge-house, and nobody knows what he did there. He was a Foundation Late at sixteen. A Core disciple at nineteen. He disappeared the year after, and the Hall let it be known that he was in seclusion, and nobody has seen his face since." He lifts the lantern. "You will be seen going into that house. I would like you not to go alone."

"Who should I take?"

"Not Feng. A Silver Leaf is a hostage in the Hall's courtyard." Qin Hao tilts his head. "Take Ye. She is an Elder. She is entitled."

"She is a scholar."

"She is a scholar who is not afraid of anything that can be written down." The ghost of a smile. "There is a great deal in the ridge-house that has been written down."

He holds out the lantern. Jian takes it.

"Go home," says the old Guard gently. "Sleep. The tea will keep. And Lin Jian."

"Elder?"

"A sky like that does not come once." Qin Hao's eyes are very old, and very kind. "It will come again, for a larger thing. You should know that before they tell you."

He walks back up the steps alone, with the card in his fist and the lantern swinging. At the base of his skull, under the wet hair, the silver mark gives one slow, cold throb, and goes still.

Locator, he thinks. Queried.

And over the roofs of the Inner Court, faint and far in the violet dusk, a single lantern comes alight on the ridge.
